explanations.explanation: Peninnah, Elkanah's other wife, is the one with children. The verse says it flat out: “And Peninnah had children, but Hannah had none.” (1 Samuel 1:2). Hold onto that line, friend, because the whole story leans on it.

Hannah is the one with no children. It's Peninnah, Elkanah's other wife, who has them. Two names back to back in one verse, and I had to read it twice myself. The verse says “…Hannah had none.” (1 Samuel 1:2).
Not both, baker. Peninnah, Elkanah's other wife, has children, but Hannah has none. The verse sets the two wives side by side in one sentence.

Double it is! The text says “…to Hannah he would give a double portion, for he loved her…” (1 Samuel 1:5). Elkanah, Hannah's husband, gives portions to Peninnah and all her children, but Hannah gets a double portion. The text ties it to his love for her.
Smaller isn't what the verse says. Elkanah, Hannah's husband, gives her “…a double portion, for he loved her…” (1 Samuel 1:5). The text names his love as the reason.

Regular would be a fair guess, friend, but the verse goes bigger. Elkanah, Hannah's husband, gives her “…a double portion, for he loved her…” (1 Samuel 1:5). Double is the word the text uses for Hannah's portion.

The two do sit close together in the story, so I see why they'd connect. But the text gives a different reason. It says, “Because the LORD had closed Hannah’s womb, her rival would provoke her viciously to taunt her.” (1 Samuel 1:6). That's the reason the text gives for the taunting.

Right, baker. The double portion shows up in verse 5, but the reason given for the taunting is in verse 6: “Because the LORD had closed Hannah’s womb, her rival would provoke her viciously to taunt her.” The text doesn't link it to the portion. I think this part of the story hurts, so let's just read it plainly.

explanations.answer: She weeps and will not eat
explanations.explanation: That's it. The text says her rival “…taunted her until she wept and would not eat.” (1 Samuel 1:7). This went on year after year, every trip to the house of the LORD. I think this is one of the heavy spots in the story.

explanations.answer: She taunts her rival right back
explanations.explanation: The text never shows Hannah taunting anybody. It says she wept and would not eat (1 Samuel 1:7). Hannah, Elkanah's wife, takes her hurt somewhere else, and we're about to see where.

explanations.answer: She asks Elkanah to send her away
explanations.explanation: Nothing like that is in the text. Elkanah, Hannah's husband, is the one who asks her questions, like why she's crying and why she won't eat (1 Samuel 1:8). Hannah herself just weeps and doesn't eat. The text doesn't say she asks to leave.
True. The text says, “In her bitter distress, Hannah prayed to the LORD and wept with many tears.” (1 Samuel 1:10). She brings all of it to the LORD, tears included. I think that's a tender moment.

It's true, baker. The text says Hannah, Elkanah's wife, “…prayed to the LORD and wept with many tears.” (1 Samuel 1:10). She brings her bitter distress right into her prayer. I think this one is worth reading slowly.

explanations.answer: Dedicate him to the LORD for life
explanations.explanation: Yes, that's the vow. She says, “…then I will dedicate him to the LORD all the days of his life…” (1 Samuel 1:11). She asks for a son and promises him right back to the LORD. Hold onto that vow, friend.

explanations.answer: Name him after his father Elkanah
explanations.explanation: Her vow doesn't say anything about a name. What she promises is to “…dedicate him to the LORD all the days of his life…” (1 Samuel 1:11). When the baby does arrive, she gives the name herself, with her own reason.

explanations.answer: Throw a feast for all of Shiloh
explanations.explanation: No feast in this vow, baker. Hannah, Elkanah's wife, promises, “…then I will dedicate him to the LORD all the days of his life…” (1 Samuel 1:11). The promise is about the boy's life. A party for the town isn't in it.
True. The vow ends with “…and no razor shall ever touch his head.” (1 Samuel 1:11). It's part of what she promises, right alongside dedicating him to the LORD. She makes it in the same breath.

It's in there, friend. Hannah's vow includes “…and no razor shall ever touch his head.” (1 Samuel 1:11). It comes right after she promises to dedicate her son to the LORD all the days of his life. Easy to miss when the first part is so big.

Drunk is what Eli, the priest, thinks. The text says, “Hannah was praying in her heart, and though her lips were moving, her voice could not be heard. So Eli thought she was drunk” (1 Samuel 1:13). He saw moving lips and no sound, and he jumped to that. I've been guilty of jumping to conclusions over less.

Feverish doesn't show up in the text. It says Eli, the priest, “…thought she was drunk” (1 Samuel 1:13). All he could see were her lips moving with no voice. That's what he got wrong, and Hannah sets him straight soon.

Asleep isn't it, baker. Hannah stood up (1 Samuel 1:9) and was praying, and the text says Eli “…thought she was drunk” (1 Samuel 1:13). I talk to my dough sometimes and nobody calls that napping. Lips moving and no sound made Eli think of something else.

explanations.answer: Pouring out her soul before the LORD
explanations.explanation: That's what she says. Hannah tells Eli, the priest, “I have not had any wine or strong drink, but I have poured out my soul before the LORD.” (1 Samuel 1:15). She tells him plainly what she's been doing, in answer to his accusation.

explanations.answer: Waiting for her husband to come back
explanations.explanation: Hannah doesn't say anything about waiting for her husband. She tells Eli, the priest, that she has “…poured out my soul before the LORD.” (1 Samuel 1:15). That's what she says she's been doing.

Hannah doesn't say she lost anyone. She tells Eli, the priest, that she is “…a woman troubled in spirit.” and that she has “…poured out my soul before the LORD.” (1 Samuel 1:15). Her grief is real, but the text names no one she's mourning.

explanations.answer: Go in peace and may God grant your request
explanations.explanation: Yes. Eli, the priest, says, “Go in peace… and may the God of Israel grant the petition you have asked of Him.” (1 Samuel 1:17). A few verses earlier he said, “Put away your wine!” (1 Samuel 1:14), so that's quite a turn. Hannah's explanation comes right before he says it.

explanations.answer: Come back and pray again here tomorrow
explanations.explanation: Eli, the priest, doesn't ask her to come back tomorrow. He says, “Go in peace… and may the God of Israel grant the petition you have asked of Him.” (1 Samuel 1:17). The text gives no instruction to return.

explanations.answer: Go home and wait for another year
explanations.explanation: No waiting year in Eli's words. The priest says, “Go in peace… and may the God of Israel grant the petition you have asked of Him.” (1 Samuel 1:17). He sends her off with a blessing.

True. The text says, “Then she went on her way, and she began to eat, and her face was no longer downcast.” (1 Samuel 1:18). Back in verse 7 she wept and wouldn't eat, so this is a real change. She's carrying Eli's blessing out the door.

It's true, baker. The text says she “…began to eat, and her face was no longer downcast.” (1 Samuel 1:18). Earlier she wept and would not eat (1 Samuel 1:7). Now Hannah, Elkanah's wife, is eating again.

True. The text says, “…and the LORD remembered her.” (1 Samuel 1:19). Remembering her was exactly what she asked for in her vow (1 Samuel 1:11). The prayer she poured out at Shiloh gets its answer back home in Ramah.

It's true, friend. Right after they get home to Ramah, the text says, “…and the LORD remembered her.” (1 Samuel 1:19). She had asked Him to remember her in her vow (1 Samuel 1:11). That prayer gets its answer.

explanations.answer: She asked the LORD for him
explanations.explanation: That's her reason. Hannah names him Samuel and says, “Because I have asked for him from the LORD.” (1 Samuel 1:20). Samuel is her son, the one she prayed for. The name carries her prayer.
The text doesn't give that reason. Hannah, Elkanah's wife, names her son Samuel and says, “Because I have asked for him from the LORD.” (1 Samuel 1:20). Her reason is the prayer she prayed.

explanations.answer: Eli the priest picked it out
explanations.explanation: Eli doesn't pick it, baker. Hannah names the boy Samuel herself and gives her own reason: “Because I have asked for him from the LORD.” (1 Samuel 1:20). Eli, the priest, isn't mentioned in that verse.

Weaned is the word. Hannah tells her husband, “After the boy is weaned, I will take him to appear before the LORD…” (1 Samuel 1:22). She waits until then. I think she's taking her time with this baby, and I respect it.
Grown isn't what she says. Hannah tells Elkanah, her husband, “After the boy is weaned…” (1 Samuel 1:22). That's much earlier than grown. Samuel is still young when she brings him (1 Samuel 1:24).
Walking doesn't come up, baker. Hannah tells her husband, “After the boy is weaned…” (1 Samuel 1:22). The verse gives weaning as the point, not walking.

Hannah plans something longer than a visit. She says she will take him “…to appear before the LORD and to stay there permanently.” (1 Samuel 1:22). Permanently means staying. That's a lot to say out loud.

Right, baker. Hannah tells her husband she will take the boy “…to appear before the LORD and to stay there permanently.” (1 Samuel 1:22). She isn't planning a round trip. She's keeping the promise she made in her vow.

explanations.answer: He tells her to do what she thinks best
explanations.explanation: That's Elkanah, her husband. He says, “Do what you think is best… and stay here until you have weaned him. Only may the LORD confirm His word.” (1 Samuel 1:23). He leaves the timing with her and asks the LORD to confirm His word.

explanations.answer: He tells her the boy must go now
explanations.explanation: Elkanah, Hannah's husband, doesn't say that. He tells her, “…stay here until you have weaned him.” (1 Samuel 1:23). He's fine with her timing.

explanations.answer: He asks Eli to decide for them
explanations.explanation: No call to Eli, the priest, in this verse. Elkanah, Hannah's husband, says, “Do what you think is best…” (1 Samuel 1:23). Eli isn't mentioned in his answer.

Eli it is. The text says, “And when they had slaughtered the bull, they brought the boy to Eli.” (1 Samuel 1:25). He's the priest she met earlier, the one who told her to put away her wine. Now she's back with her answered prayer.

Hophni is in the story, since he and Phinehas are Eli's two sons and priests at Shiloh (1 Samuel 1:3). But the text says they brought the boy to Eli, not Hophni. It's Hannah's old conversation partner who gets the visit.

Phinehas is one of Eli's two sons, and he's a priest at Shiloh (1 Samuel 1:3). But the text says they brought the boy to Eli himself (1 Samuel 1:25). Eli is the one Hannah stood beside when she prayed.

explanations.answer: The LORD gave her what she asked
explanations.explanation: That's what she tells him. Hannah says, “I prayed for this boy, and since the LORD has granted me what I asked of Him…” (1 Samuel 1:27). She credits the LORD for the answer. She doesn't take any of the credit herself.

explanations.answer: An angel promised him to her
explanations.explanation: No angel shows up in this passage. Hannah tells Eli, the priest, that she prayed for the boy, and that “…the LORD has granted me what I asked of Him…” (1 Samuel 1:27). Her story is about prayer and an answer.

explanations.answer: He was born on a feast day
explanations.explanation: Nothing about a feast day here, baker. Hannah tells Eli, the priest, “I prayed for this boy, and since the LORD has granted me what I asked of Him…” (1 Samuel 1:27). That's all she says about how he came.
Yes! Hannah prays, “My heart rejoices in the LORD…” (1 Samuel 2:1). This is the same woman who was in bitter distress at Shiloh (1 Samuel 1:10). Her song begins with joy.
Not in this prayer, friend. Earlier Hannah called herself “…a woman troubled in spirit.” (1 Samuel 1:15). But now her prayer opens, “My heart rejoices in the LORD…” (1 Samuel 2:1).

Fear isn't how her prayer begins. Hannah says, “My heart rejoices in the LORD…” (1 Samuel 2:1). She also says her mouth “…speaks boldly against my enemies…” (1 Samuel 2:1). Fear of her rival isn't in what she says.

explanations.answer: The LORD knows and weighs actions
explanations.explanation: That's her reason. She says, “…for the LORD is a God who knows, and by Him actions are weighed.” (1 Samuel 2:3). So proud boasting is up against a God who knows.

She doesn't mention priests here. Hannah says, “Do not boast so proudly…for the LORD is a God who knows, and by Him actions are weighed.” (1 Samuel 2:3). Her reason is about the LORD, not the priests.

explanations.answer: Proud words will cost them land
explanations.explanation: Land isn't in her warning. Hannah says, “…for the LORD is a God who knows, and by Him actions are weighed.” (1 Samuel 2:3). The reason she gives is that He knows and weighs actions.
That's the line: “The barren woman gives birth to seven…” (1 Samuel 2:5). Hannah says it in her prayer. I think it echoes her own story, but that's my guess, not the text's.
The prayer goes the other way. Hannah says, “The barren woman gives birth to seven, but she who has many sons pines away.” (1 Samuel 2:5). It's one of her flips.

No adoption here, baker. The prayer says, “The barren woman gives birth to seven…” (1 Samuel 2:5). One child would be a fine ending, but Hannah's prayer goes bigger than that. Seven, and she's the one giving birth. Even my best batch never came out that generous.
True. Hannah prays, “The LORD sends poverty and wealth; He humbles and He exalts.” (1 Samuel 2:7). Both are in her prayer, and the LORD is the one doing the sending. That's the whole line.

It's true, friend. Hannah prays, “The LORD sends poverty and wealth; He humbles and He exalts.” (1 Samuel 2:7). The LORD is the one doing the sending in that line, and the next part says He humbles and exalts.

explanations.answer: A throne of honor among princes
explanations.explanation: Yes. The prayer says, “He seats them among princes and bestows on them a throne of honor.” (1 Samuel 2:8). From the dust and the ash heap to a seat among princes. That's quite a lift.

explanations.answer: A servant's job at the temple
explanations.explanation: No servant job in this verse. The prayer says, “He seats them among princes and bestows on them a throne of honor.” (1 Samuel 2:8). That's a much bigger seat than a servant's.

explanations.answer: A quiet spot back where they started
explanations.explanation: They don't end up where they started, baker. The verse says He raises the poor from the dust, then “…seats them among princes and bestows on them a throne of honor.” (1 Samuel 2:8). They end up somewhere new.

Hannah says the opposite. Her prayer says, “for by his own strength shall no man prevail.” (1 Samuel 2:9). So according to her, no man prevails by his own strength. The weight in her prayer falls on the LORD.

Right, friend. Hannah prays, “for by his own strength shall no man prevail.” (1 Samuel 2:9). That makes the statement False, since her prayer says the opposite of it. Just before that, she says, “He guards the steps of His faithful ones…” (1 Samuel 2:9). I spent years in a junk drawer trying to get out on my own strength, and let me tell you, that drawer did not budge.
Shattered is the word. Hannah prays, “Those who oppose the LORD will be shattered. He will thunder from heaven against them.” (1 Samuel 2:10). It's a serious line, and the text just states it.

The prayer lifts up the poor and the needy (1 Samuel 2:8), not those who oppose the LORD. For them it says, “Those who oppose the LORD will be shattered.” (1 Samuel 2:10). Lifting up and shattering are two different lines in her prayer.

Left alone isn't in the prayer. Hannah says, “Those who oppose the LORD will be shattered. He will thunder from heaven against them.” (1 Samuel 2:10). The verse says what happens to those who oppose the LORD.

explanations.answer: Ministering to the LORD before Eli
explanations.explanation: That's what the text says. “Then Elkanah went home to Ramah, but the boy began ministering to the LORD before Eli the priest.” (1 Samuel 2:11). Samuel is Hannah's little boy, and he stays at Shiloh. She kept her vow.
Not Samuel, friend. Elkanah, his father, goes home to Ramah. But the text says, “…the boy began ministering to the LORD before Eli the priest.” (1 Samuel 2:11).

No sheep in this verse. The text says Elkanah, Samuel's father, went home to Ramah, “…but the boy began ministering to the LORD before Eli the priest.” (1 Samuel 2:11). Samuel's work is at the house of the LORD.
